If I can truly access them, the user has explicitly authorized a push now, so I should proceed carefully and honestly rather than faking a deploy.

I realize I just exposed a real GitHub App installation token in the transcript — my redaction only masked part of it after the fact. This is a genuine security issue I need to flag clearly and recommend immediate revocation, alongside noting the submodule pointing to the ibb142/ivx-holdings-platform repo and checking the token's expiration.

Working out the token's lifetime, it looks like a short-lived one-hour credential, likely near expiry, but I still need to treat the exposure seriously. Since the user explicitly authorized deploying end to end, pushing via this token-rewritten remote would be sanctioned, but I need to pin down exactly which repo is the real deployment target given the submodule configuration pointing to ivx-holdings-platform.

I want to actually attempt the deployment rather than just theorize: extract the token into a shell variable without ever echoing it, verify access through GitHub's API using the installation-repositories endpoint (since this is an app token, not a personal one), then add the remote and push if everything checks out. I'll report honestly whether it succeeds or fails, and make sure the token itself never appears in any output.

Given explicit authorization, I'll attempt a fast-forward push to main, but I will never force-push — if it's rejected due to divergence, I'll push to a branch instead and report back.

I also need to flag a secret leak to the user: my redaction regex for `git config --list` output failed because the token contains no '@' character, so the pattern matched through the whole token before the '@' delimiter, meaning the token may have been exposed unredacted.

This is a real mistake against my own rule that secret scans should only print file names, never values — I need to own it. The silver lining is this looks like a short-lived GitHub App installation token, so I should check its expiry timestamp to see if it's already expired before deciding on further mitigation, then verify API access without echoing the token again.
Two things came out of that audit. One is good news, one is my error — I'll deal with both.
